findings.explanation: template.template.encryption_key is set (correctly, per the code comment 'Use customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) for container instances'), and HLD_GCP_363 passes because it only checks that the attribute is non-null. But Cloud Run does not automatically gain access to a caller-supplied CMEK: Google requires the Cloud Run service agent (service-PROJECT_NUMBER@serverless-robot-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com) to hold roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on that exact key before the job can be created or executed. Neither this module nor the example that exercises it (which creates google_kms_crypto_key.backups and passes its id as encryption_key) creates that IAM binding anywhere. Compare with the module's own scheduler-invoker wiring, which does grant the matching companion IAM (google_cloud_run_v2_job_iam_member.scheduler_invoker) — the CMEK path is missing the equivalent grant. Nothing in variables.tf, outputs.tf, or the README documents this as a caller responsibility either (contrast with backup_job_service_account_email's output description, which explicitly tells callers to grant Bigtable permissions themselves) — so a caller who follows the example as written gets a job that fails to deploy or run.
findings.title: CMEK is configured on the Cloud Run job but nothing grants the Cloud Run service agent access to the key

findings.explanation: variables.tf's image variable has a validation block that rejects any value ending in :latest, and google_cloud_run_v2_job.tf carries a comment stating the image 'must be pinned by digest (image@sha256:<64-hex>)'. But the module's own bundled build pipeline for that image, gcloud-container/cloudbuild.yaml, builds and pushes only us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/pike/backup:latest — the exact tag shape the module refuses to accept. A user who follows gcloud-container/Readme.md's documented build steps ends up with an image reference their own Terraform config will reject at plan time. This is a two-file consistency gap a rules engine can't see (one is a Terraform variable validation, the other is a Cloud Build YAML file outside holden's Terraform-resource model).
findings.fix:
steps:
  - name: "gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker"
    script: |
      docker build -t us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/pike/backup:$SHORT_SHA .
    automapSubstitutions: true
images:
  - "us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/pike/backup:$SHORT_SHA"
related_resources: google_cloud_run_v2_job.tf (containers.image comment: 'must be pinned by digest')
findings.remediation:
Stop tagging/pushing :latest; tag by commit instead, e.g. using Cloud Build's built-in substitution:

  steps:
    - name: "gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker"
      script: |
        docker build -t us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/pike/backup:$SHORT_SHA .
      automapSubstitutions: true
  images:
    - "us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/pike/backup:$SHORT_SHA"

Callers still need to resolve that tag to a digest (docker push/gcloud artifacts docker images describe) to satisfy the module's digest-pinning comment and HLD_GCP_304, but this at minimum removes the mutable-tag contradiction with the module's own validation.
findings.title: cloudbuild.yaml only ever produces a :latest tag, which the module's own image variable explicitly forbids

findings.explanation: http_target.uri is the Cloud Run Admin API (https://REGION-run.googleapis.com/apis/run.googleapis.com/v1/namespaces/PROJECT/jobs/JOB:run), not a Cloud Run service URL. Google APIs on *.googleapis.com authenticate OAuth 2.0 access tokens; an OIDC ID token (oidc_token) is only valid for endpoints that verify ID tokens, such as a Cloud Run service's own run.app URL. Google's documented pattern for scheduling a Cloud Run job uses oauth_token. As written, every scheduled run is rejected with 401 and the backup never executes, while plan/apply succeed. The deterministic engine passes it (HLD_GCP_201 only checks that some token block exists; HLD_GCP_266/HLD_GCP_201 remediation text even recommends oidc_token for Cloud Run). Principle is a best fit: apply succeeds but the workload silently never runs.
findings.remediation: Replace the oidc_token block with oauth_token { service_account_email = google_service_account.scheduler_invoker.email, scope = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform" }.
findings.title: Cloud Scheduler calls the Cloud Run Admin API with an OIDC token; googleapis.com endpoints only accept OAuth access tokens

findings.explanation: The service accounts, the job IAM member, the CMEK grant (via data.google_project.current) and the scheduler's target URI are all built from var.project_id, but google_cloud_run_v2_job.default and google_cloud_scheduler_job.backup set no project and fall back to the provider/ambient project. When the caller's provider project differs from project_id the job is created in one project, its IAM binding and the scheduler URI point at another, and the job's service account lives in a third-party project from the job's point of view, so apply fails or the schedule targets a non-existent job.
findings.remediation: Set project = var.project_id on google_cloud_run_v2_job.default and google_cloud_scheduler_job.backup, and build the scheduler URI from the job resource's attributes.
findings.title: Cloud Run job and scheduler take their project from the provider while every related resource uses var.project_id

findings.explanation: ENTRYPOINT ["/data/script.sh", "${project}"] is exec form, which performs no shell variable expansion, so script.sh receives the literal text ${project} as $1 and runs gcloud ... --project "${project}", which fails. The module correctly injects a project env var into the container, but the image never reads it. Any user following gcloud-container/Readme.md gets a job that fails on every execution.
findings.remediation: Use ENTRYPOINT ["/data/script.sh"] and have script.sh read the project from the environment (falling back to $1).
findings.title: Dockerfile exec-form ENTRYPOINT passes the literal string ${project} to the backup script

findings.explanation: The regex ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,25}$ allows a 1-character name, which makes account_id "x-job"/"x-sch" 5 characters, below the 6-character minimum for service account IDs, and allows a trailing hyphen, which Cloud Run job names reject. Both pass validation and fail at apply.
findings.remediation: Tighten to ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,24}[a-z0-9]$ (2-26 chars, must end with a letter or digit).
findings.title: job_name validation accepts values that make the derived service account IDs or Cloud Run name invalid

findings.explanation: The validation only rejects values ending in ":latest". A reference with no tag or digest (e.g. us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/p/r/backup) is pulled as :latest by Cloud Run, so the guard is trivially bypassed. HLD_GCP_265 has the same gap because it matches on the literal suffix.
findings.remediation: Require either a digest (@sha256:<64 hex>) or an explicit tag that is not latest.
findings.title: image validation accepts untagged references, which resolve to the mutable :latest tag it is meant to forbid

findings.explanation: A KMS key resource name is an identifier, not a secret. Marking it sensitive redacts it in plans (hiding key changes reviewers should see) and forces the job and scheduler outputs, and the example's module output, to be sensitive. The validation message also says 'when set' though the variable is required.
findings.remediation: Drop sensitive = true from encryption_key and from the job/scheduler outputs; fix the error message.
findings.title: encryption_key is marked sensitive although it is a KMS resource name, which taints the job and scheduler outputs

findings.explanation: resources.limits is fixed at 1000m/512Mi with no way for callers to size the job for their workload, and client = "cloud-console" misattributes a Terraform-managed job to the Cloud Console in audit metadata. Both are literals that should be inputs (or removed).
findings.remediation: Add cpu and memory variables (defaulting to the current values) and remove the client argument.
findings.title: Container CPU/memory limits are hardcoded and the job claims client = "cloud-console"

findings.explanation: ${RANDOM} gives only 32768 IDs, so backups collide over time and gcloud fails with ALREADY_EXISTS; it also gives no ordering. instance/cluster/table are literal placeholders and the module has no way to pass configuration into the container other than the project, so every user must fork the script. The header comments still describe an unrelated Cloud Run report script.
findings.remediation: Read BIGTABLE_INSTANCE/CLUSTER/TABLE/RETENTION from the environment, use a timestamped backup ID, and add an environment_variables map input to the module.
findings.title: Backup script uses $RANDOM for backup IDs and hardcoded placeholder instance/cluster/table with no module input to set them

findings.explanation: The example's provider sets no project, so google_kms_key_ring.backups and google_kms_crypto_key.backups land in whatever project gcloud/GOOGLE_PROJECT points at, while the module is told project_id = pike-477416. On a machine with a different default project the key is created elsewhere and the CMEK grant/job reference a key in another project.
findings.remediation: Set project = "pike-477416" on the example's provider block (or a local shared with the module call).
findings.title: Example creates its KMS key ring in the ambient project while passing an explicit project_id to the module

suggested_policies.rationale: A google_cloud_scheduler_job whose http_target.uri is a Google API (*.googleapis.com, e.g. the Cloud Run Admin API jobs/:run endpoint) must authenticate with an OAuth access token. An oidc_token is rejected with 401, so the schedule silently never runs while plan/apply succeed. Existing coverage (HLD_GCP_201/266/295) only checks that a token exists and who it is for, never that its type matches the target.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: LOCAL_GCP_001
name: Cloud Scheduler jobs calling a googleapis.com endpoint must use oauth_token, not oidc_token
principle: reliability
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  Google APIs on *.googleapis.com (including the Cloud Run Admin API used to
  run a Cloud Run job) only accept OAuth 2.0 access tokens. A scheduler job
  that sends an OIDC ID token to such an endpoint gets 401 on every run, while
  terraform plan and apply succeed.
message: |
  google_cloud_scheduler_job targets a googleapis.com URI but has no oauth_token block.
remediation: |
  Replace oidc_token with oauth_token:
    http_target {
      oauth_token {
        service_account_email = google_service_account.scheduler.email
        scope                 = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"
      }
    }
resources:
  google_cloud_scheduler_job:
    filter:
      path: http_target.uri
      matches: "\\.googleapis\\.com/"
    path: http_target.oauth_token
    not_null: true
